messages.author: f5d35c1292532224
messages.subject: Bifactor latent mean difference
parts:
Dear Colleagues

Let us say that we have a model with nine indicators (assumed continuous) that is modelled as a bifactor model with three group factors (so all items load on the general factor and one respective group factor). I am interested in the latent mean score difference on the general factor for a binary group. Would it suffice to use the group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts") with std.lv = T to get the standardized mean score difference? I tried the measEQ.syntax in semTools and it warned me:

 "a factor's mean cannot be freed unless it has at least one indicator without a cross-loading whose intercept is constrained to equality".

The model syntax for group means sets the two latent means of GEN to 0:

## LATENT MEANS/INTERCEPTS:

A ~ c(alpha.1.g1, alpha.1.g2)*1 + c(0, 0)*1
B ~ c(alpha.2.g1, alpha.2.g2)*1 + c(0, 0)*1
C ~ c(alpha.3.g1, alpha.3.g2)*1 + c(0, 0)*1
GEN ~ c(alpha.4.g1, alpha.4.g2)*1 + c(0, 0)*1

Is it then possible to examine latent mean score differences of the general factor in the bifactor model, and if so, must the group factor means for A, B, C be set to (0, 0) or could it be (0, NA) instead?

Thank you very much.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Bifactor latent mean difference
parts: Is it then possible to examine latent mean score differences of the general factor in the bifactor model

It is possible, but arbitrary.  Because the means of your observed variables are each influenced by the means of 2 latent variables, there is not enough information in the data to distinguish between differences due to the general factor and differences due to the specific factor.
must the group factor means for A, B, C be set to (0, 0) or could it be (0, NA) instead?

That would arbitrarily identify your model, so you could estimate the group-2 general-factor mean (difference).  But that would only be valid if the specific-factor means do not differ between groups, which you cannot verify.  The possibility of finding a solution provides no protection against the potential (and likely) invalidity of that solution.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
